clue.text: Stuttering, so we mangled — these?

indicators.note: the letters are mangled into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters

explanation.surface: Someone asks what phrases could leave a speaker stammering and garbling their words.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: tongue twisters are exactly what make us stutter and mangle words, and the fodder even rearranges into them.
explanation.definitionFit: Tongue twisters are phrases designed to trip speakers into stuttering and mangling them.

clue.text: What's travelled quickly, leading to stir?

definitions.text: What's travelled quickly, leading to stir?

indicators.note: the first piece comes before the second

parts.note: to tear = to rush; 'has torn along' = has travelled quickly
ado = fuss, a stir

explanation.surface: A riddle about something fast-moving that leaves commotion in its wake.
explanation.walkthrough: TORN is the past participle of tear in its sense of rushing, not ripping. The whole clue then describes a tornado: a fast-moving thing that causes a stir.
explanation.definitionFit: A tornado is a fast-travelling storm that leaves upheaval behind it.

clue.text: Thieves in prisons

definitions.meaning: read as a verb: he thieves = he steals, in British slang
the nick is British slang for prison

explanation.surface: A plain statement that robbers end up behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thieves' reads as a plural noun but is the verb: he thieves, he nicks. In British slang 'the nick' is a prison or police station.
explanation.definitionFit: To nick is British slang for to steal, and a nick is slang for a jail.

clue.text: Marks given to Mötley Crüe?

parts.note: the surface wants grades or review scores awarded to a band; the setter means printed marks attached to letters
look at the band's name as printed: two decorative double dots, over the o and the u

explanation.surface: A question about what score or rating a rock band receives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marks' suggests grades or reviews for the heavy-metal band Mötley Crüe, but the marks are the decorative double dots in the band's printed name.
explanation.definitionFit: An umlaut is the two-dot mark placed over a vowel, as in ö and ü.

clue.text: Equipment swap? Quite the reverse!

parts.note: equipment = tools, swap = trade: an exchange of gear is a 'trade of the tools'
swap the two nouns in that phrase round, and it becomes a set phrase that itself means equipment

explanation.surface: Someone proposes exchanging gear, then corrects themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: Equipment = tools and swap = trade, so an equipment swap is a trade of tools; 'quite the reverse' flips the phrase into tools of the trade, which really does mean equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: The tools of the trade are the equipment needed for a particular job.

clue.text: Everyman increasingly intoxicated, overheard in warmer part of Europe

indicators.note: we catch the words by ear, not by spelling

parts.note: Everyman, the setter, is I; more drunk is beerier

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to getting drunker and drunker on holiday in southern Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pseudonym stands for 'I', a common self-reference. Said together, 'I beerier' is a close match for the peninsula's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Iberia is the peninsula of Spain and Portugal, in Europe's warm south-west.

clue.text: Bill reduced slightly, Morse's colleague (Geordie) wanting cheapest plonk

indicators.note: a slight reduction takes just the last letter off

parts.note: a tab is a bill, as at a bar
Sergeant Lewis, Inspector Morse's sidekick, loses his final S
a Geordie comes from Newcastle, in the North East (NE) of England

explanation.surface: A detective's sidekick, on a tight budget, asks for the cheapest bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: Inspector Morse is a British TV detective whose sergeant is Lewis. A Geordie is someone from Tyneside, so the clue points to NE for North East England.
explanation.definitionFit: Table wine is ordinary everyday wine, the cheap end of the list; plonk is slang for cheap wine.

clue.text: Find new direction for overture, not very flowing

indicators.note: tells us to leave out the next piece
the remaining letters run into a new shape

parts.note: OVERTURE without V (very)

explanation.surface: A composer is told the overture drags and needs a new direction.
explanation.walkthrough: V for very is a standard abbreviation. Musical words like overture and flowing make it read like a note to a composer.
explanation.definitionFit: To reroute is to send something by a new course or direction.

clue.text: Footwear from scaly reptile

definitions.meaning: a brand of chunky foam clog
short for the big river reptile with the snapping jaws

explanation.surface: Shoes made out of crocodile skin.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures crocodile-leather shoes, but the footwear is the foam Croc clog, and 'from' only joins the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A Croc is a brand of foam clog, and croc is short for crocodile.

clue.text: The Spanish tucked into chocolate snack before tango with songwriter

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside another
this piece comes ahead of the next

parts.note: a Lion bar is a British chocolate bar
el = 'the' in Spanish, placed inside LION|BAR
T in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone eats a chocolate bar before dancing a tango with a songwriter.
explanation.walkthrough: A Lion bar is a chocolate snack sold in Britain. Lionel Bart wrote the musical Oliver!
explanation.definitionFit: Lionel Bart was the English songwriter behind the musical Oliver!

clue.text: Sixth to recognise fool's gold, somewhere in the Bahamas

indicators.note: take the sixth letter of the next word

parts.note: sixth letter of RECOGNISE
an ass is a fool
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: Someone learns to tell pyrite, fool's gold, from the real thing while in the Bahamas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool's gold' is a set phrase for pyrite, but here it splits into two pieces: fool and gold.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Nassau, the capital, is one place in the Bahamas among many.

clue.text: Malicious, up itself play

indicators.note: the letters are played with, moved around

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses a pretentious play as nasty and self-regarding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up itself' is British slang for conceited, which makes the surface read as a theatre review.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiteful means wanting to hurt or annoy: malicious.

clue.text: Theatrical farce no one gets rid of (though second character cut)

indicators.note: remove the second letter of the phrase

parts.note: as printed
I = one, the Roman numeral

parts.words: gets rid of (though second character cut)
parts.note: SEES OFF = gets rid of, without its second letter E

explanation.surface: A farce that no one can shake off, even with a character written out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' suggests a role in the play, but it means a letter. Noises Off is Michael Frayn's backstage farce.
explanation.definitionFit: Noises Off is Michael Frayn's 1982 farce about a theatre company.

clue.text: Still, I can dance a little

indicators.note: the letters move about into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: An ageing dancer insists they can still manage a few steps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A little' reads as the amount of dancing still possible, which hides it as the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A scintilla is a tiny trace or amount: a little.

clue.text: In announcement, name location on the web

indicators.note: the word is spoken, so we go by its sound

parts.note: to cite is to name, as a source

explanation.surface: A web address is read out in a public announcement.
explanation.walkthrough: The spoken word for naming a source sounds the same as the answer but is spelt with a C.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for website, the everyday word for a page's place on the internet.

clue.text: Fry — and damage

definitions.meaning: a noun: one French fry, in British English
knock a small piece off a cup or plate

explanation.surface: Cooking something and spoiling it at once.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a chip is what Americans call a French fry.
explanation.definitionFit: A chip is a fried potato stick, and to chip is to break a small piece off.

clue.text: Honesty also seen in court? Not quite

indicators.note: this piece sits inside the next
the word falls just short: drop its last letter

parts.note: COURT without its last letter
and = also, placed inside C|OUR

explanation.surface: Asking whether honesty is also on display in a courtroom, and deciding it isn't really.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not quite' looks like a verdict on the court's honesty; it trims the last letter off COURT.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: frankness and openness in speech.

clue.text: Humiliated Head of Communications was anxious

indicators.note: take the first letter of the next word

parts.note: first letter of Communications
'I hastened to add' = I was anxious to add, eager

explanation.surface: An office head of communications was left humiliated and nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head of Communications' looks like a job title; it only supplies the letter C. 'Was anxious' is in the sense of being keen to do something.
explanation.definitionFit: Chastened means humbled or subdued after a rebuke: humiliated.

clue.text: Smear last bit of oil into power tool

indicators.note: take the final letter of the next word

parts.note: a sander smooths wood by power

indicators.note: that letter goes inside the next piece

parts.note: last letter of OIL, placed inside S|ANDER

explanation.surface: An instruction to oil a power tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smear' looks like part of the oiling job, but it is the definition, in its sense of damaging someone's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To slander is to smear someone with false spoken claims.

clue.text: Secretly listens in on (bugs)

definitions.meaning: insects, not listening devices: pincered creepy-crawlies

explanation.surface: Someone eavesdrops, the bracket adding that they do it with listening devices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' looks like a gloss on the spying, as in hidden microphones, but it is a second definition: the insects.
explanation.definitionFit: To earwig is informal British for to eavesdrop; earwigs are also pincered insects.

clue.text: Both sides of Atlantic flipping over party puzzle

indicators.note: each piece is turned back to front
the pieces go over, around, the next piece

parts.note: the US on one side, the UK on the other, each flipped to SU and KU
a do is a party, placed between SU and KU

explanation.surface: Americans and Britons alike go head over heels for a party game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' applies to each country separately, not to the whole string, so the party ends up sandwiched in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudoku is a number-placement puzzle on a nine-by-nine grid.

clue.text: Advise against ructions (in part)

indicators.note: the answer is part of the letters in front of us

parts.note: agaINST RUCTions

explanation.surface: Someone counsels against rows breaking out.
explanation.walkthrough: A ruction is a noisy quarrel or disturbance.
explanation.definitionFit: To instruct someone can mean to advise or direct them.

clue.text: Some out-drank a rake in Turkish city

indicators.note: only some of the letters are used

parts.note: out-drANK A RAke

explanation.surface: A drinker out-boozes a debauched man-about-town in a Turkish bar.
explanation.walkthrough: A rake is an old word for a dissolute pleasure-seeker, which fits the drinking scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain fit: the capital of Turkey is a Turkish city.

clue.text: Kinaesthetically immaculate Russians' orchestrated variations, primarily?

definitions.text: Kinaesthetically immaculate Russians' orchestrated variations, primarily?

indicators.note: take the first letter of each word

parts.note: first letters of each word

explanation.surface: A description of flawless Russian dancers performing orchestral variations.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kirov is the famous St Petersburg ballet company, now called the Mariinsky, so the whole clue also describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kirov Ballet is renowned for precise Russian dancers performing to orchestral scores.

clue.text: Playwright's retrospective to depict old, cold Spanish kingdom

indicators.note: looking backwards: read the assembled string back to front

parts.note: to draw = to depict
o = old, as in OE for Old English
C for cold, as on a tap
León was a medieval kingdom in Spain

explanation.surface: A retrospective of a playwright's work depicting an old, cold Spanish realm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrospective' looks like an exhibition of the playwright's life; here it tells us to read DRAWOCLEON backwards. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Noël Coward was the English playwright of Private Lives and Blithe Spirit.

clue.text: A wading bird in a bar

definitions.meaning: a secretive marsh bird, relative of the coot and crake
a rod, as for hanging towels, not a pub

explanation.surface: A bird wanders into a pub, the setup of a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'bar' of the surface is a pub; the definition means a rod or rail.
explanation.definitionFit: A rail is both a marsh-dwelling wading bird and a horizontal bar.

clue.text: Cut-off trousers and vest are, surprisingly, items of great value

indicators.note: the end of the next word is cut away
the letters turn up in an unexpected order

parts.note: TROUSERS without its last letter
rest of the fodder; 'and' joins the pieces

explanation.surface: Someone discovers that their old cut-offs and vest are worth a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut-off trousers' reads as shorts, but the hyphenated word tells us to trim TROUSERS. A vest in Britain is an undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A treasure trove is a hoard of valuables, anything of great worth.
